pynimation
  • Event bindings
  • View page source

Event bindings

Event bindings are used to register functions that will be called on user events like mouse motion, mouse click, key presses, etc.

Events

Events are specified as pygame Event objects.
The type attribute describes whether it is a mouse motion event, a key press, a key release etc.
The dict attribute holds different values depending on the type of motion, for example which key is pressed, with which modifier, or which mouse button is pressed
See the pygame documentation on events, keyboard and mouse for a complete reference
For example, an event matching the l key being pressed can be created with:
e = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_l})

Note

Pressing the l key with any modifier will not trigger this event

To match the l key being pressed while the CTRL modifier is pressed, we can write:
e = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_l, "mod": pg.KMOD_NONE | pg.KMOD_CTRL})

Adding bindings

The EventManager class is responsible for keeping current event bindings, listening to user events and calling event handlers appropriately
Bindings can be be modified either with the bind(), unbind() and rebind() functions, or by setting the bindings attribute.

With bind()

With the bind() function, a single binding can be added with:
# event handler
def translateCharacter(character: Character, trans: np.ndarray=[0,0,0]) -> None:
    character.globalTransform.translate(trans)


event = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_h})

v.eventManager.bind(event, translateCharacter, args=[character], kwargs={"trans":, [0.1, 0, 0]})
This code binds the translateCharacter function to the k key press. The function will be called with character as a first argument and [0.1,0,0] as a value for the trans keyword argument. It will be called anytime a the user presses the k key

With the bindings attribute

A tuple of all current bindings is available through the bindings attribute of the EventManager class.
In this tuple, event bindings are represented by Binding objects, containing a pygame event, and a partial object.
A partial object contains a function and a set of values for its arguments, it is directly callable, and it will call the function with the set of values. For example, a partial object equivalent to the handler of the last example can be constructed with:
partialHandler = partial(translateCharacter, character, trans=[0.01, 0, 0])

Warning

Tuples are immutable. So modifying the bindings tuple directly will not work. To modify the bindings this way, construct a new Tuple with modified bindings and assign it to the bindings attribute

A Binding object can then be constructed and added to existing bindings with:
# construct binding object
binding = Binding(
    event, [partialHandler]
)

# construct the new tuple of bindings
newbindings = (*v.eventManager.bindings, binding)

# set the new tuple of bindings
v.eventManager.bindings = newbindings

Accessing the runtime Event

pygame events received at runtime sometime contain additional information that can be useful for the handler. For example a pg.MOUSEMOTION event received when the user moves the mouse contains a rel and a pos property inside its dict attribute that gives the position of the mouse and its relative position since the last mouse motion event.
To retrieve these informations, a handler can name one of its parameters event, and the EventManager will set its value to the Event received at runtime when calling the handler.
For example, to print the current mouse position:
# print position of the mouse when it moves
def printMousePos(event: Optional[Event] = None) -> None:
    if event is not None and "pos" in event.dict:
        print(event.pos)


mouseevent = Event(pg.MOUSEMOTION, {})

v.eventManager.bind(event, printMousePos)

Example

from typing import Optional
from functools import partial
import numpy as np
import pygame as pg
from pygame.event import Event
from pynimation.io import load
from pynimation.viewer import Viewer
from pynimation.viewer import Binding
from pynimation.viewer import Character
from pynimation.common import data as data_

bvh_file = data_.getDataPath("data/animations/Walk_loop.bvh")

[animation] = load(bvh_file)
character = Character(animation)

v = Viewer()

# get the list of bindings
bindings = v.eventManager.bindings
print([str(b) for b in bindings])


# bind a handler to an event
def translateCharacter(character: Character, trans: np.ndarray) -> None:
    character.globalTransform.translate(trans)


event = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_h})
v.eventManager.bind(event, translateCharacter, args=[character, [0.1, 0, 0]])


# if the handler has a keyword argument named "event", it will take the value
# of the Event received at runtime. It is useful to get additional information
# on the event
def printMousePos(event: Optional[Event] = None) -> None:
    if event is not None and "pos" in event.dict:
        print(event.pos)


mouseevent = Event(pg.MOUSEMOTION, {})
v.eventManager.bind(mouseevent, printMousePos)

# rebind all handlers bound to an event to another
newevent = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_j})
v.eventManager.rebind(event, newevent)

# rebind a specific handler bound to an event to another (in case multiple handlers)
newevent = Event(pg.KEYDOWN, {"key": pg.K_j})
v.eventManager.rebind(newevent, event, translateCharacter)

# unbind all handlers bound to an event
v.eventManager.unbind(event)

# unbind a specific handler bound to an event (in case multiple handlers)
v.eventManager.unbind(mouseevent, printMousePos)

# bindings can also be modified and added by setting the tuple of bindings of the
# eventManager
# for this, Bindings objects are constructed, with handlers given as partial objects
# a partial object contains a function and a set of values for its arguments
# it is directly callable, it will call the function with the set of values
binding = Binding(
    event, [partial(translateCharacter, character, [0.01, 0, 0])]
)
mousebinding = Binding(mouseevent, [partial(printMousePos)])

# construct the new tuple of bindings
newbindings = (*v.eventManager.bindings, binding, mousebinding)

# set the tuple of bindings
v.eventManager.bindings = newbindings

v.display(character)
